evidence: Cic. Off. 3.75: quī rē vērā nōn esset hērēs
M-O s.v. really: rē vērā, rēapse
terms.comment: The fact set against words or appearances. Rē alone does the same against verbō: “in word … in fact”.

terms.gloss: actually (correcting what was said): no, rather; on the contrary
evidence: Sen. Ep. 47.1: ‘servī sunt.’ immō hominēs.
Cic. Off. 3.90: Immō vērō obsecrābit patrem
terms.comment: The “actually” of a correction. Never an answer on its own, unlike minimē: it always brings the corrected statement (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Rep. 1.2: rēapse, nōn ōrātiōne (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: An old word, not found after Cicero (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 123: tametsī verbō nōn audeat, tamen rē ipsā (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: Late Latin for “actively”, from āctuālis, “active, practical” (Macr.). It never means “in fact”.

terms.gloss: but surely (raising an objection), not “what I mean is”
evidence: Traupman p. 103: what I mean is (in correcting a misunderstanding), at enim
Plaut. Trin. 3.3.78: at enim nimis hīc longō sermōne ūtimur (Lewis & Short s.v. at)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: at enim introduces an objection, “but certainly, but surely”, usually one the speaker expects from someone else. To correct what was said or understood, Latin uses immō (above).

phrases.latin: et quidem multō parcius scrīpsī quam rē vērā furere eōs invēnī
phrases.english: and indeed I wrote much more mildly than the frenzy I actually found them in

phrases.latin: ‘servī sunt.’ immō hominēs. ‘servī sunt.’ immō contubernālēs.
phrases.english: “They’re slaves.” No, actually, they’re people. “They’re slaves.” No, actually, they share our roof.

phrases.latin: silēbitne fīlius? Immō vērō obsecrābit patrem, nē id faciat
phrases.english: will the son say nothing? Actually, no: he will beg his father not to do it
